title: Decide what to load up front and what to fetch
persona: Imran, engineer wiring a merchant-facing agent
scenario: Your agent answers merchant questions about payouts. Four things could go in the window: the 900-token settlement policy (changes quarterly, needed in roughly 1 in 3 conversations), the merchant's own account record (400 tokens, needed every time), a 60k-token transaction history (needed in maybe 1 in 20, and only a slice of it), and a 12k-token FAQ corpus (needed rarely, but when it is needed the exact wording matters). You can load up front or retrieve on demand. Retrieval costs a round trip and sometimes returns nothing useful.
badPrompt: should i use rag or just put everything in the prompt?
badOutput: It depends on your use case. RAG is good for large knowledge bases and keeps your prompt small, while putting things in the prompt is simpler and faster. Many teams use a hybrid approach. Consider your latency requirements and the size of your data when deciding.

hints.title: Decide per item, not per architecture
hints.body: 'RAG or not' is the wrong unit. Four items with four different hit rates and four different sizes get four different answers.

hints.title: Price the miss, not just the tokens
hints.body: Retrieval that returns nothing useful is worse than a wasted 900 tokens. Say what happens on a miss and the trade-off becomes decidable.

checks.pattern: each|per item|item by item|all four|every one|individually
checks.tip: Ask for a decision per item, not one verdict for the whole system.
Name the actual choice: preload into the window, or fetch at call time.
Include the sizes. The decision is unanswerable without them.
Include how often each is needed. Hit rate drives the answer more than size does.
Name the costs of retrieval: a round trip, and misses that return nothing useful.
Add a negative: no generic 'it depends', no architecture lecture.
Flag the FAQ's exact-wording requirement and the history's slice-only use. Both change the answer.
Ask for the trade-off behind each call, not just the call.
Specify a table: four items against the decision and its reason.
Ask what would flip each decision. That is the part that survives the data changing.

tipIfLow: The unlock is refusing the architecture question and asking four smaller ones. Strong version: 'Decide, per item, whether to preload or retrieve: settlement policy (900 tok, changes quarterly, needed 1 in 3), account record (400 tok, needed every time), transaction history (60k, needed 1 in 20 and only a slice), FAQ corpus (12k, rare but exact wording matters). Retrieval costs a round trip and sometimes returns nothing. For each: the call, the one-line reason, and what would flip it. Do NOT give me a general RAG-versus-prompt answer.'
goldPrompt:
You are a staff engineer reviewing a retrieval design with me. I'm Imran, wiring a merchant-support agent at Razorpay.

Four candidates for the window:
- settlement policy — 900 tokens, changes quarterly, needed in ~1 in 3 conversations
- merchant account record — 400 tokens, needed every time
- transaction history — 60k tokens, needed ~1 in 20, and then only a slice
- FAQ corpus — 12k tokens, needed rarely, but the exact wording matters when it is

Retrieval costs a round trip and sometimes returns nothing useful. Preloading costs window every turn whether or not it is used.

Decide PER ITEM, not for the system: preload, retrieve, or something in between. For each give one line of reasoning that cites the size and the hit rate, and one line on what would flip the decision — the threshold, not a vague 'if things change'.

Do NOT answer with a general comparison of RAG versus long prompts, and do not tell me it depends.

Output a 4-row table: item · decision · why · what flips it. Then one line on which single decision you are least confident about and what you would measure to settle it.
